new: he lashed his horses
reason: Butler: "As he spoke he lashed his horses"; accepted Book 3 keeps "lashed" in the same chariot formula (B03-P037 "He lashed the horses on"), and D29 restores Butler's word.

old: Then Pisistratus urged his horses forward, and they flew ahead willingly enough.
new: Then Pisistratus lashed his horses on, and they flew forward readily enough.
reason: Butler: "Pisistratus lashed his horses on and they flew forward nothing loth", the same line as B03-P037, which accepted Book 3 (candidate-v3) prints "Pisistratus lashed the horses on and they flew forward readily enough" (its README asserts 'readily enough' x2); "willingly enough" is Butler's own phrase for Clytemnestra at B03-P023, and "urged ... forward" drops the lash.

old: my father is Odysseus—or was, if he ever lived.
new: my father is Odysseus, as surely as he ever lived.
reason: Butler: "my father is Ulysses, as surely as that he ever lived" is an asseveration; "or was, if he ever lived" turns it into doubt about whether Odysseus is alive, or ever existed, and adds "or was".

new: have all of you murdered
reason: Butler: "would have all of you murdered"; "killed" softens violence (the rules forbid it), and accepted Book 11 keeps Butler's "murder" throughout.

old: who had been feasting with my father in his official capacity
new: who had been feasting with my father as his attendants
reason: Butler: "guests who had been feasting with my father, as being in attendance on him"; the guests are his attendants, while "in his official capacity" invents a detail and attaches it to the father.

new: At this Theoclymenus
reason: Butler: "On this Theoclymenus called him apart"; the binding brief rule is that sentence-opening "At this" takes no comma, as ¶24 of this draft already has it.

new: his unhappy father
reason: Butler: "his unhappy father" (ill-fated); "troubled" suggests anxiety, which is a different quality.

old: I hope nothing valuable has been stolen from the house while you’ve been gone
new: I hope nothing valuable has been taken from the house in spite of you
reason: Butler: "taken from the house in spite of you" means against your will; "while you’ve been gone" changes the sense to a matter of timing.

old: Let me also tell you something else you should know.
new: Let me also tell you about another matter you had better attend to.
reason: Butler: "another matter which you had better attend to"; the draft drops the call to act on it.

new: I hardly think they’ll succeed
reason: Butler: "I do not much think they will succeed"; the hedge is lost.

new: will send you a fair wind
reason: Butler: "will send you a fair wind"; ¶24 of this draft and accepted Books 11–12 print "a fair wind", so the Book renders one formula two ways.

new: Zeus sent them a fair wind
reason: Butler: "Jove sent then a fair wind"; this should match ¶24 and accepted Books 11–12, "a fair wind".

new: a golden goblet of wine
reason: Butler: "a golden goblet of wine"; he keeps goblet apart from the "gold cup" of ¶5 and the "double cup" of ¶7, and accepted B10-P024 keeps "golden goblet".

old: a bird flew on their right
new: a bird flew on his right
reason: Butler: "a bird flew on his right hand" and later "on their right hands"; the first "his" is Telemachus's, and the draft makes both "their".

old: and took heart, and Pisistratus said
new: and took heart. At that Pisistratus said
reason: Butler: "whereon Pisistratus said"; GLOSSARY (Book 4 row) renders whereon "at that", as accepted B12-P011 does, and "and" drops the consequence.

new: fetch you
reason: Butler: "he will come down here to fetch you"; "himself" is an added intensifier.

new: a seer fleeing from Argos
reason: Butler: "a seer"; accepted B09-P038, B10-P044 and B11-P022 keep "seer" (D29: Butler's own word).

old: the greatest prophet in the world
new: the greatest seer in the world
reason: Butler: "the greatest seer in the whole world"; same reason as the first "seer" in this paragraph.

new: in great distress of mind both because
reason: Butler: "in much distress of mind"; "suffering greatly" drops the fact that the distress is mental, which the rest of the clause ("haunted by a great sorrow") relies on.

new: because of a woman’s gifts
reason: Butler: "by reason of a woman’s gifts"; he writes "bribes" in the parallel at B11-P042 and "gifts" here, and the draft flattens the two into one.

new: Eos, goddess of the dawn, enthroned in gold,
reason: Butler: "Aurora, throned in gold"; Eos (D5 widened: Aurora→Eos) appears only here in the edition, while everywhere else the goddess is "Dawn", so a listener cannot identify her without a short gloss at first use.

old: and then returned to the ship. She took me by the hand
new: and then returned to the ship. At that she took me by the hand
reason: Butler: "went back to the ship, whereon she took me by the hand"; the draft drops the connective, which should be "at that" per GLOSSARY's Book 4 row.

old: a good feast with meat and wine
new: a good dinner with meat and wine
reason: Butler has "dinner" twice in this paragraph; the draft restores the first and changes the second to "feast".

new: Zeus alone in heaven, however, knows
reason: Butler: "Jove, however, in heaven alone knows"; "however" marks the turn from praising Eurymachus to his possible doom.

old: “With that she returned to the house.
new: “At this she returned to the house.
reason: Butler: "On this she went back to the house"; the binding brief rule renders Butler's sentence-opening "On this" as "At this" (as ¶24 and ¶43 do).
